title: Insect stings and bites: first aid
asks: bee sting what do I do
how to treat a wasp sting
stinger still in my skin how to get it out
how do I remove a tick
tick on me how to pull it off
answer: First watch for a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis): difficulty breathing, dizziness, swelling of the face or throat, or a widespread rash. If any of these appear, seek immediate medical attention.

For a severe allergic reaction, if an epinephrine (adrenaline) auto-injector is available: help the person use it, or give it yourself if you are allowed and trained, and call for medical help. For the signs and the full steps, ask for the severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) card.
Fire ants: move away from the ants, and remove any clothing or jewelry that may have ants trapped in it, because they can keep stinging.
Stinger left in the skin (bees, wasps): remove it as quickly as possible. Gently scrape it off with a blunt edge such as a credit card or your fingernail, and avoid squeezing the venom sac.
Wash the area with mild soap and water. Be gentle.
Apply a cold compress, or an ice pack wrapped in a cloth, for 10 to 15 minutes at a time, several times a day, for pain, swelling and itching.

For itching and inflammation, over-the-counter creams, ointments or sprays with hydrocortisone, calamine or antihistamine can help. If itching or swelling persists, an over-the-counter oral antihistamine can be taken. Follow the instructions on the package.
Do not scratch the bite: scratching can cause further irritation and infection.

Tick: grasp it with fine-tipped tweezers as close to the skin as possible and pull upward gently and steadily with even pressure. Do not twist or jerk it, and avoid squeezing or crushing its body. Then clean the bite area thoroughly with soap and water or an antiseptic.
warnings: An insect bite or sting can cause great pain, allergic reaction, inflammation and infection, and some may cause serious illness or even death if not treated correctly. In any case, medical personnel should examine the person at the earliest possible time.
If the insect is unknown, or symptoms are severe or getting worse, consult a health care professional.
After a tick bite, fever, rash, joint pain or flu-like symptoms need evaluation by a health care professional.

quotes.text: An insect bite or sting can cause great pain, allergic reaction, inflammation, and infection. If not treated correctly, some bites or stings may cause serious illness or even death. When an allergic reaction is not involved, first aid is a simple process. In any case, medical personnel should examine the casualty at the earliest possible time.

Remove the stinger (if applicable): In the case of stinging insects like bees or wasps, it's important to remove the stinger as quickly as possible to prevent further venom injection. Gently scrape it off the skin using a blunt edge like a credit card or your fingernail. Avoid squeezing the venom sac, as it may release more venom.
Wash the bite area: Clean the bite site with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Be gentle and avoid excessive scrubbing.

Apply a cold compress: To alleviate pain, reduce swelling, and minimize itching, apply a cold compress or an ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the bite area. Do this for 10-15 minutes at a time, several times a day.

Use over-the-counter remedies: Over-the-counter topical creams, ointments, or sprays containing ingredients such as hydrocortisone, calamine lotion, or antihistamines can help relieve itching and inflammation. Follow the instructions and precautions on the product packaging.

Take oral antihistamines: If itching or swelling persists, you can take over-the-counter oral antihistamine to help reduce allergic reactions and relieve symptoms. Consult a pharmacist or health care professional for appropriate dosage and recommendations.
Avoid scratching: Although it may be tempting, refrain from scratching the insect bite to prevent further irritation, infection, or the development of a secondary skin condition.

Monitor for severe reactions: In rare cases, insect bites can cause severe allergic reactions, known as anaphylaxis. If you experience symptoms such as difficulty breathing, dizziness, swelling of the face or throat, or a widespread rash, seek immediate medical attention.
The treatment of anaphylactic shock is urgent and time sensitive. Immediate actions include calling for medical help and, if available, using the casualty's epinephrine auto-injector.

If anaphylactic shock is suspected, immediate medical assistance is crucial. The primary treatment involves administering epinephrine (adrenaline). If an epinephrine auto-injector is available, assist the affected individual in using it, or administer it yourself if you are allowed and trained.
If the insect type is unknown or if the Service member is experiencing severe or worsening symptoms, it is best to consult a health care professional for proper evaluation and guidance.
Move away from the area where the ants are present to avoid further stings. • Remove any clothing or jewelry that may have ants trapped in them, as they can continue to sting.

Prepare for tick removal: Use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick as close to the skin's surface as possible. Avoid squeezing or crushing the tick's body. • Remove the tick: Gently and steadily pull the tick upward with even pressure. Do not twist or jerk it. The goal is to remove the entire tick, including its mouthparts. Dispose of the tick by placing it in a sealed bag or container or by submerging it in alcohol. • Clean the bite area: Thoroughly clean the bite area with soap and water or an antiseptic solution to reduce the risk of infection.

If in an area where these diseases are prevalent or if you develop symptoms such as fever, rash, joint pain, or flu-like symptoms after a tick bite, it is crucial to consult a health care professional for proper evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment.

conflict: No disagreement found between sources. Added in revision: the auto-injector line comes from ATP 4-02.11's anaphylactic shock paragraphs (7-32 and 7-35), not from its insect section (16-48), which says only to 'seek immediate medical attention'; WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care 2018 likewise says to give intramuscular adrenaline as soon as possible for a severe allergic reaction with difficulty breathing. Dose, repeat doses and positioning are on the anaphylaxis card, with their source disagreements. The answer is now ordered steps (kind 'protocol'); the fire-ant line was moved up because ATP 4-02.11 para 16-76 puts moving away from the ants first. MULTIPLE STINGS: the ask 'multiple stings when to worry' was dropped. The kit says only that fire ants 'may attack simultaneously, leading to multiple stings' (ATP 4-02.11 para 16-76) and gives no guidance on how many stings are dangerous.

review.notes: Re-review 2026-11-25 (claude-opus-5-5 xhigh). Both previous findings fixed: A2 adds the epinephrine auto-injector step from ATP 4-02.11 7-32/7-35 with a pointer to the anaphylaxis card (conflict says it is not from the insect section); kind is now protocol and the steps are in a sound order (fire ants first, per ATP 16-76). The multiple-stings ask, which the kit cannot answer, was dropped and conflict says why. Checked in context: ATP 4-02.11 16-43 onward (stinger, wash, cold 10-15 min, creams, oral antihistamine, no scratching, anaphylaxis signs, unknown insect, fire ants, ticks) and ATP 3-50.21 bites and stings (same tick method, so no conflict). All remaining asks answered; no PDF junk. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 (xhigh), independent review 2026-11-24) Problems: (1) Point (d): A1 tells the reader only to 'seek immediate medical attention' for anaphylaxis. The single most important action, using an epinephrine auto-injector if one is available, is missing; ATP 4-02.11 7-35: 'If an epinephrine auto-injector is available, assist the affected individual in using it, or administer it yourself if you are allowed and trained.' (ATP's prevention list also says people allergic to stings should 'be prepared with the proper medication'.) Fix: add that line and a pointer to the anaphylaxis card. (2) Point (b): the answer is ordered steps (watch for anaphylaxis, remove the stinger, wash, cold compress, creams, antihistamine); kind should be 'protocol'. Confirmed: ATP 4-02.11 16-43 onward (stinger scraping, wash, cold compress 10-15 min, OTC creams, oral antihistamine, no scratching, anaphylaxis signs, unknown insect or worsening = professional, fire ants, tick removal and cleaning, tick-borne disease symptoms). No PDF junk. Minor: 'multiple stings when to worry' is claimed but not addressed; no kit quote found on multi-sting toxicity, so either drop that ask or answer it only with W2's 'severe or worsening symptoms'.
